```{r}
set.seed(100)
```

## Hypothesis Test for Population Proportion (Two-Tailed)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 26.1"}
Let $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ be independent and identically distributed Bernoulli random variables with probability of success $p$. Assume we want to test the hypothesis $H_0: p = p_0$ vs $H_A: p \neq p_0$ and we want the Type-I error rate to be no larger than $\alpha$. Then we would reject $H_0$ when the following was true:

$$
\frac{\hat{p}-p_0}{\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}} < z_{\alpha/2} \quad \text{ or } \quad \frac{\hat{p}-p_0}{\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}} > z_{1-\alpha/2}
$$

More succinctly, we can reject $H_0$ when $\left|\frac{\hat{p}-p_0}{\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}} \right| > z_{1-\alpha/2}$.
:::

## Hypothesis Test for Population Proportion (Left-Tailed)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 26.2"}
Let $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ be independent and identically distributed Bernoulli random variables with probability of success $p$. Assume we want to test the hypothesis $H_0: p = p_0$ vs $H_A: p < p_0$ and we want the Type-I error rate to be no larger than $\alpha$. Then we would reject $H_0$ when the following was true:

$$
\frac{\hat{p}-p_0}{\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}} < z_{\alpha}
$$
:::

## Hypothesis Test for Population Proportion (Right-Tailed)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 26.3"}
Let $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ be independent and identically distributed Bernoulli random variables with probability of success $p$. Assume we want to test the hypothesis $H_0: p = p_0$ vs $H_A: p > p_0$ and we want the Type-I error rate to be no larger than $\alpha$. Then we would reject $H_0$ when the following was true:

$$
\frac{\hat{p}-p_0}{\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}} > z_{1-\alpha}
$$
:::

## P-Value for Population Proportion (Two-Tailed)

For a two-tailed test involving the proportion ($H_A: p \neq p_0$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\hat{P}-p}{\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}} \geq \left|\frac{\hat{p}-p}{\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}} \right| \Bigg| p = p_0\right)
$$

## P-Value for Population Proportion (Left-Tailed)

For a left-tailed test involving the proportion ($H_A: p < p_0$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\hat{P}-p}{\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}} \leq \frac{\hat{p}-p}{\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}} \Bigg| p = p_0\right)
$$

## P-Value for Population Proportion (Right-Tailed)

For a right-tailed test involving the proportion ($H_A: p > p_0$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\hat{P}-p}{\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}} \geq \frac{\hat{p}-p}{\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}} \Bigg| p = p_0\right)
$$

## Ex: Exam

::: {.callout title="Example 26.1"}
You administer an exam with 40 questions to a student and record whether they got each question right or wrong. You find that the student got 34 of the questions correct. You want to test if the true probability $p$ of responding correctly to a question is less than 0.9. Conduct a hypothesis test at the 5% significance level.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 40
p_hat <- 34/n
p0 <- 0.9
alpha <- 0.05
z_statistic <- (p_hat - p0)/sqrt(p0*(1-p0)/n)

cat("The z-statistic is: ", z_statistic, ", the critical value is: ", qnorm(alpha), ", and the p-value is: ", pnorm(z_statistic), sep = "")
```

## Ex: Survey

::: {.callout title="Example 26.2"}
A survey is conducted to estimate the proportion of customers who are satisfied with a new product. Out of 120 respondents, 82 report being satisfied. You want to test if the true proportion $p$ of satisfied customers is different from 0.78. Conduct a hypothesis test at the 10% significance level.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 120
p_hat <- 82/n
p0 <- 0.78
alpha <- 0.1
z_statistic <- (p_hat - p0)/sqrt(p0*(1-p0)/n)

cat("The z-statistic is: ", z_statistic, ", the critical value is: ", qnorm(1-alpha/2), ", and the p-value is: ", 2*pnorm(-abs(z_statistic)), sep = "")
```

## Ex: Light Bulbs

::: {.callout title="Example 26.3"}
A manufacturer inspects a random sample of 75 light bulbs from a production line and finds that 15 are defective. You want to test if the true proportion $p$ of defective bulbs is greater than 0.1. Conduct a hypothesis test at the 1% significance level.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 75
p_hat <- 15/n
p0 <- 0.1
alpha <- 0.01
z_statistic <- (p_hat - p0)/sqrt(p0*(1-p0)/n)

cat("The z-statistic is: ", z_statistic, ", the critical value is: ", qnorm(1-alpha), ", and the p-value is: ", 1-pnorm(z_statistic), sep = "")
```

## Ex: Charitable Donations

::: {.callout title="Example 26.4"}
A charity organization surveys 120 randomly selected households and finds that 36 of them have donated to charity in the past year. You want to test if the true proportion $p$ of households that donate is less than 0.4. Conduct a hypothesis test at the 5% significance level.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 120
p_hat <- 36/n
p0 <- 0.4
alpha <- 0.05
z_statistic <- (p_hat - p0)/sqrt(p0*(1-p0)/n)

cat("The z-statistic is: ", z_statistic, ", the critical value is: ", qnorm(alpha), ", and the p-value is: ", pnorm(z_statistic), sep = "")
```

## Ex: Pets

::: {.callout title="Example 26.5"}
A pet store surveys 150 customers and finds that 45 own at least one pet. You want to test if the true proportion $p$ of customers who own pets is different from 0.35. Conduct a hypothesis test at the 1% significance level.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 150
p_hat <- 45/n
p0 <- 0.35
alpha <- 0.01
z_statistic <- (p_hat - p0)/sqrt(p0*(1-p0)/n)

cat("The z-statistic is: ", z_statistic, ", the critical value is: ", qnorm(1-alpha/2), ", and the p-value is: ", 2*pnorm(-abs(z_statistic)), sep = "")
```

## Ex: Personality Test

::: {.callout title="Example 26.6"}
A company offering personality tests conducts a survey of 200 individuals and finds that 50 have taken the test. You want to test if the true proportion $p$ of individuals who take the personality test is greater than 0.2. Conduct a hypothesis test at the 5% significance level.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
n <- 200
p_hat <- 50/n
p0 <- 0.2
alpha <- 0.05
z_statistic <- (p_hat - p0)/sqrt(p0*(1-p0)/n)

cat("The z-statistic is: ", z_statistic, ", the critical value is: ", qnorm(1-alpha), ", and the p-value is: ", 1-pnorm(z_statistic), sep = "")
```
